summary: Describes how to create a conference using SIP URI-list services. A user agent client gives a conference server the initial list of participants by including a URI list in the INVITE request. The server can then invite everyone on the list. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
SIP is the protocol a phone or a video app uses to start a call. To set up a conference, a client normally asks a conference factory for a new conference, waits for the answer, and only then invites the people who should be in it.

This document lets the client do both in one step. The client puts the list of participants in the invitation itself, and the conference server invites them as soon as it has created the conference.

questions: how to invite multiple participants in sip
how to create a sip conference with a uri list
what does copycontrol bcc mean in sip
subtitle: Lets a SIP client create a conference and name the first participants in a single INVITE request.

tldr.problem: Creating an ad hoc SIP conference normally takes two rounds: the client sends an INVITE to a conference factory URI and gets back the real conference URI, then adds participants one by one. Some environments need the conference created and the participant list supplied in a single operation.
tldr.mechanism: The client puts the participants in a recipient-list body inside the first INVITE and adds the recipient-list-invite option tag to its Require header. The conference server creates the conference, then invites everyone on the list, including an anonymized URI list in each outgoing INVITE so recipients can see who else is there.
tldr.outcome: One request now creates the conference and starts the invitations. The extension applies only to the initial INVITE to the conference factory URI: a re-INVITE sent to the conference URI is rejected with 420 (Bad Extension).

facts.label: Media type of the URI list

today: RFC 5366 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the recipient-list-invite SIP option-tag, registered in the Option Tags subregistry under the SIP parameter registry, and it builds on the URI-list service framework of RFC 5363.

sections.title: Creating a Conference in One Request
sections.content:
Section 5.4 of RFC 4579 describes how to create a conference using ad hoc SIP methods of RFC 3261. The client sends an INVITE request to a conference factory URI and receives the actual conference URI, which contains the isfocus feature tag, in the Contact header field of a response, typically a 200 (OK) response. Once the User Agent Client has that conference URI, it can add participants to the newly created conference in the several ways described in RFC 4579.

Some environments have tough requirements about how quickly a conference must be set up. They require the User Agent Client to be able to request the creation of an ad hoc conference and to give the conference server the initial set of participants in a single operation. This document describes how to meet that requirement, using the mechanism for transporting URI lists in SIP messages that is defined in RFC 5363.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a conference the ordinary way takes two steps and two round trips. This document combines them into one request, which matters when the conference has to exist quickly.

sections.title: User Agent Client Procedures
sections.content:
A User Agent Client that wants to include the set of initial participants in its initial INVITE request to create an ad hoc conference adds a body whose disposition type is recipient-list, as defined in RFC 5363, with a URI list containing the participants that the User Agent Client wants the conference server to invite. The User Agent Client MUST also include the recipient-list-invite option-tag, which is registered with IANA in Section 8, in a Require header field, and it sends this INVITE request to the conference factory URI.

The INVITE transaction is also part of an offer/answer exchange that establishes a session between the User Agent Client and the conference server, as specified in RFC 4579. The INVITE request may therefore need to carry a multipart body: a session description and a URI list.

The status code in the response does not say whether the conference server was able to bring the users in the URI list into the conference. A 200 (OK) response means that the conference was created successfully, that the User Agent Client that generated the INVITE request is in the conference, and that the server understood the URI list. If the client wants information about the status of the other users in the conference, it SHOULD use general conference mechanisms, such as the conference package defined in RFC 4575.

Once the dialog between the User Agent Client and the conference server has been established, the client can send subsequent INVITE requests, typically called re-INVITE requests, for example to change the characteristics of the media exchanged with the server. There are no semantics associated with recipient-list bodies in re-INVITE requests, although future extensions may define them, so User Agent Clients SHOULD NOT include such bodies in re-INVITE requests sent to a conference server. The difference between the two kinds of request matters here: the initial INVITE goes to the conference factory URI, while the re-INVITE goes to the URI the server supplied in a Contact header field when the dialog was established. From the client's point of view, the resource identified by the first URI supports recipient-list bodies, while the resource identified by the second does not.
sections.plainLanguage: The client attaches two things to the invitation: the list of people to invite, and a marker saying that the list is there. The server's reply confirms that the conference was created and that the list was understood, but it says nothing about whether each person answered. A later invitation inside the same call must not carry the list again, because the conference server does not support it there.

sections.title: The URI-List Document Format
sections.content:
As described in RFC 5363, specifications of individual URI-list services, such as the conferencing service described here, need to specify a default format for recipient-list bodies used within the particular service.

The default format for recipient-list bodies for conferencing User Agents is the XML resource list format specified in RFC 4826, extended with the copy control attribute extension defined in RFC 5364. Conferencing User Agents generating recipient-list bodies MUST support both of these formats and MAY support other formats, and conferencing servers able to handle such bodies MUST support both of these formats and MAY support others.

Each URI can be tagged with a copyControl attribute set to either to, cc or bcc, indicating the role in which the recipient will get the INVITE request. URIs can also be tagged with the anonymize attribute, to prevent the conference server from disclosing the target URI in a URI list. The same extension defines a recipient-list-history body, which contains the list of recipients, and the default format for those bodies is the same XML resource list document extended with the copy control extension.

The XML resource list document provides features, such as hierarchical lists and the ability to include entries by reference relative to the XCAP root URI, that the conferencing service does not need, since it only needs to transfer a flat list of URIs between a User Agent and the conference server. Conferencing User Agents SHOULD therefore use flat lists and SHOULD NOT use entry-ref elements, and a conference factory application receiving a URI list with more information than that MAY discard all the extra information. Figure 1 of the RFC shows a flat list with three entries, one tagged to, one cc and one bcc.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of people is written as an XML document. Each entry says whether the person is a main recipient, a copied recipient or a blind copy, and can ask for the address to be hidden from the other participants. The conferencing service only needs a flat list, so the richer features of the XML format should not be used.

sections.title: Conference Server Procedures
sections.content:
Conference servers that are able to receive and process INVITE requests with a recipient-list body SHOULD include the recipient-list-invite option-tag in a Supported header field when responding to OPTIONS requests.

On reception of an INVITE request containing a recipient-list body as described in Section 3, a conference server MUST follow the rules described in RFC 4579 to create the ad hoc conference. Once the conference is created, the server SHOULD attempt to add the participants in the URI list to the conference as if their addition had been requested using any of the methods described in RFC 4579. Once it has created the conference and attempted to add the initial set of participants, the conference server behaves as a regular conference server and MUST follow the rules in RFC 4579.

The incoming INVITE request contains a URI-list body or reference, as specified in RFC 5363, with the actual list of recipients. If this list includes resources tagged with the copyControl attribute set to to or cc, the conference server SHOULD include a URI list in each of the outgoing INVITE requests, formatted according to the XML format for resource lists and the copy control extension. The URI-list service MUST follow the procedures specified in RFC 5364 for the handling of the anonymize, count and copyControl attributes.

If the conference server includes a URI list in an outgoing INVITE request, it MUST include a Content-Disposition header field, specified in RFC 2183, with the value set to recipient-list-history and a handling parameter, as specified in RFC 3204, set to optional.

For a re-INVITE request there are no semantics associated with recipient-list bodies, so a conference server that receives one, and therefore a recipient-list-invite option-tag, rejects it following standard SIP procedures with a 420 (Bad Extension), which carries an Unsupported header field listing the recipient-list-invite option-tag. The resource identified by the conference URI does not support the extension, while the resource identified by the conference factory URI does, and consequently includes the option-tag in, for example, responses to OPTIONS requests.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server gets the invitation with the list, it creates the conference and then sends its own invitation to each person on the list. Each outgoing invitation carries a copy of the list, with the hidden addresses replaced and the blind-copy recipients removed, so that everyone can see who else is in the room.

sections.title: Example Exchange
sections.content:
Figure 2 of the RFC shows the example operation. A User Agent Client sends an INVITE request, F1, containing an SDP body and a URI list to the conference server. The conference server answers with a 200 (OK) response and generates an INVITE request to each of the User Agent Servers identified by the URIs in the list. Each outgoing INVITE request contains SDP and a manipulated URI list.

Figure 3 shows the F1 request itself. It carries a multipart/mixed body composed of two other bodies: an application/sdp body that describes the session and an application/resource-lists+xml body that contains the list of target URIs. The request also carries Require: recipient-list-invite and a Content-Disposition: recipient-list header on the list body. The list holds seven entries: two tagged to, two tagged cc and two tagged bcc, with three of them also carrying cp:anonymize="true".

Figure 4 shows the outgoing F3 request. The application/resource-lists+xml body in it is not the same as the one in F1: the conference server has anonymized the URIs tagged with the anonymize attribute and has removed the URIs tagged with a bcc copyControl attribute. The two anonymized to entries collapse into one entry for sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid carrying a cp:count="2" attribute, and the anonymized cc entry into one carrying cp:count="1". The body is marked Content-Disposition: recipient-list-history; handling=optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a client sending one invitation that carries both the session description and the list of seven people. The server then invites each of them separately, and the list it passes on shows only the recipients that are meant to see each other, with hidden addresses replaced by a placeholder that says how many were hidden.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both conferencing and URI-list services have their own security requirements. Conferences generally have authorization rules about who can or cannot join, what type of media can or cannot be used, and so on, and this information is used by the focus to admit or deny participation. It is RECOMMENDED that these authorization rules be used to provide security for a SIP conference.

For that authorization information to be used, the focus needs to be able to authenticate potential participants, using normal SIP mechanisms such as Digest authentication and certificates. The conference-specific security requirements are discussed further in RFC 4245 and RFC 4353.

For conference creation using a list there are additional considerations. Because a conference server sending INVITE requests to a set of users acts as a URI-list service, implementations of conference servers that handle lists MUST follow the security-related rules in RFC 5363. Those rules include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorization of clients.
sections.plainLanguage: A conference has rules about who may join and what media may be used, and the server enforces them. Because the server is now inviting a list of people on its own, it must also follow the security rules that apply to any service that sends invitations to a list.

sections.title: The recipient-list-invite Option Tag
sections.content:
This document defines the recipient-list-invite SIP option-tag. It has been registered in the Option Tags subregistry under the SIP parameter registry. The description used in the registration reads: the body contains a list of URIs that indicates the recipients of the SIP INVITE request.

The option-tag is what makes the extension detectable. A client puts it in the Require header field of the INVITE request, so a server that does not understand it answers with an error instead of quietly ignoring the list. A server that does understand it announces the tag in the Supported header field when it answers an OPTIONS request.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag in the Require header is how a client tells the server that the list is not optional. A server that does not know the tag rejects the request instead of dropping the list, and a server that does know it advertises the tag when asked what it supports.

messages.label: F1 INVITE
messages.note: Carries an SDP body and the URI list.

messages.label: F2 200 OK
messages.note: The conference was created and the client is in it.

messages.label: F3 INVITE
messages.note: With SDP and a manipulated URI list.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<resource-lists xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists"
              xmlns:cp="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol">
  <list>
    <entry uri="sip:bill@example.com" cp:copyControl="to"  />
    <entry uri="sip:joe@example.org" cp:copyControl="cc" />
    <entry uri="sip:ted@example.net" cp:copyControl="bcc" />
  </list>
</resource-lists>
